articles.title: IFCE: 14 novos cursos técnicos e inscrições abertas no Ceará | G1
articles.standfirst: Novas formações serão ofertadas em oito cidades do Ceará, com opções de modalidades Integrado ao Ensino Médio e Subsequente.
articles.summary: Novas formações serão ofertadas em oito cidades cearenses, com opções de modalidades Integrado ao Ensino Médio e Subsequente.
articles.body:
O Instituto Federal do Ceará (IFCE) aprovou a criação de 14 cursos técnicos que serão ofertados em oito municípios . As novas formações são voltadas a áreas variadas, que incluem tecnologia da informação, negócios e serviços. Sete dos cursos já estão com processos seletivos abertos, e os outros sete devem ter editais lançados em breve.

Os cursos novos são em duas modalidades: Integrado ao Ensino Médio, para egressos do Ensino Fundamental; e Subsequentes, para egressos do Ensino Médio.

Segundo a instituição federal de ensino, as novas formações contribuem para a verticalização da oferta de ensino nos campi e se beneficiam da infraestrutura, do corpo docente e da experiência já existentes em cada unidade.

Veja abaixo a lista completa dos novos cursos:

Baturité : Técnico Subsequente em Panificação

Fortaleza : Técnico Integrado em Saneamento; Técnico Integrado em Tradução e Interpretação de Libras; Técnico Subsequente em Desenvolvimento Comunitário e Técnico Subsequente em Serviços de Restaurante Bar

Jaguaruana : Técnico Integrado em Programação para Jogos Digitais

Maranguape : Técnico Integrado em Eletrônica e Técnico Integrado em Inteligência Artificial

Mombaça: Técnico Integrado em Administração e Técnico Integrado em Informática

Paracuru : Técnico Integrado em Redes de Computadores

Tabuleiro do Norte : Técnico Integrado em Informática para Internet e Técnico Subsequente em Vendas

Ubajara : Técnico Integrado em Gastronomia

IFCE aprova 14 novos cursos técnicos em oito cidades — Foto: IFCE/Divulgação

Ainda conforme o IFCE, há outros 16 cursos técnicos em processo de criação. A expectativa da instituição é de que essas formações sejam finalizadas pela Pró-Reitoria de Ensino a tempo de lançarem os processos seletivos em 2027.

articles.title: Petrolina: cursos e oficinas gratuitas para jovens em outubro | G1
articles.standfirst: Atividades incluem oficinas, palestra, curso e ações sobre desenho, educação financeira, gastronomia, tecnologia e cidadania. Programação é voltada para pessoas de 15 a 29 anos.
articles.summary: Petrolina oferece cursos gratuitos e oficinas de desenho, educação financeira e design digital na Estação das Juventudes para pessoas de 15 a 29 anos em outubro.
articles.body:
Petrolina tem programação gratuita para jovens com oficinas, curso e palestra em outubro — Foto: Divulgação/Ascom PMP

A Estação das Juventudes, em Petrolina , no Sertão de Pernambuco, promove durante o mês de outubro uma programação gratuita voltada para jovens de 15 a 29 anos. A agenda reúne oficinas, palestra, curso e outras atividades relacionadas a criatividade, educação financeira, gastronomia, tecnologia e cidadania.

A programação começa nesta quinta-feira (8), das 14h às 17h, com a oficina “Desenhe o Seu Mundo: Oficina de Iniciação ao Desenho Artístico”. A atividade terá 20 vagas e propõe o uso do desenho como forma de observar, pensar e registrar o mundo ao redor.

No dia 15, das 14h às 17h, será realizada a palestra “O futuro que você quer viver começa nas escolhas que você faz hoje”, sobre educação financeira. A atividade abordará organização do dinheiro, escolhas de consumo e cuidados para evitar armadilhas financeiras.

Já no dia 20, das 8h às 12h, será realizada a oficina “Do Dendê ao Lucro”, que reúne o preparo do acarajé e noções de empreendedorismo e gestão de negócios.

A programação também inclui o Curso de Design Digital, iniciado em setembro e com aulas previstas até o dia 26 de outubro. A formação acontece de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 12h, e apresenta ferramentas de design e Inteligência Artificial aplicadas à produção de materiais e ao dia a dia.

O curso oferece auxílio-transporte de R$ 250, lanche, material didático e certificado de conclusão de 100 horas. No dia 24, às 9h, a Estação das Juventudes participa de uma ação pelo Dia dos Professores, na Escola Antônio Padilha, com apoio à emissão da Identidade Jovem.

As atividades acontecem na Estação das Juventudes, localizada na BR-407, nº 571, Cohab Massangano, próxima ao Samu. As inscrições podem ser feitas presencialmente, de segunda a sexta-feira, das 8h às 17h, enquanto houver vagas.

Outras informações podem ser obtidas pelos telefones (87) 3983-6477 e WhatsApp (87) 99212-9449.

articles.title: É falsa foto de eleitores de vermelho com tornozeleira eletrônica | G1
articles.standfirst: Detector da OpenAI, dona do ChatGPT, aponta uso de ferramentas de inteligência artificial da empresa. Além disso, conteúdo tem distorções comuns a registros fabricados sinteticamente.
articles.summary: Foto tem distorções comuns em imagens produzidas com inteligência artificial; detector da OpenAI, dona do ChatGPT, aponta que conteúdo foi criado com ferramentas de IA da empresa.
articles.body:
É #FAKE foto de eleitores vestidos de vermelho com tornozeleira eletrônica; trata-se de IA — Foto: Reprodução

Circula nas redes sociais uma foto que supostamente mostraria pessoas usando tornozeleiras eletrônicas e roupas vermelhas enquanto aguardavam em uma fila de votação nas eleições deste domingo (4). É #FAKE .

Publicada no X e no Threads , a imagem mostra três pessoas vestidas de vermelho em uma fila de votação, sendo dois adultos usando tornozeleira eletrônica e uma criança com uma camiseta estampada com o número 13. "Pega visão dos eleitores" , diz a caixa de texto sobreposto à foto.

Um post do X, que atingiu mais de 1,5 milhão de visualizações, diz: "Petistas mais fracos" .

Embora o material tenha recebido uma nota da comunidade dizendo que "A imagem é comprovadamente alterada por inteligência artificial", na seção de comentários há mensagens de pessoas que acreditaram na veracidade da cena. Veja dois exemplos: "Coitada dessa criança" ; e "A imagem já fala por si só, olha o nível" .

O Fato ou Fake submeteu a foto ao detector de inteligência artificial da OpenAI , dona do ChatGPT , que consegue identificar imagens criadas com ferramentas de IA da própria empresa. Veja o resultado da verificação (e o infográfico mais abaixo) : "Gerado com ferramentas da OpenAI. Os sinais abaixo fornecem evidências que corroboram este resultado: SynthID detectado. Credenciais de conteúdo não detectadas".

O Fato ou Fake submeteu a imagem ao detector de inteligência artificial da OpenAI, que apontou conteúdo sintético — Foto: Reprodução

O SynthID é uma tecnologia que insere uma marca d'água para identificar conteúdos sintéticos. Essa espécie de selo é incorporada a fotos fabricadas com IA. Embora imperceptível para humanos, a técnica é detectável pelo sistema.

O segundo apontamento ("Não encontramos um manifesto C2PA confiável proveniente da OpenAI") é uma referência à sigla para "Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity" (ou "Coalizão para a Proveniência e Autenticidade de Conteúdo", em português).

Criado por uma organização sem fins lucrativos nos Estados Unidos, o projeto estabelece padrões técnicos globais para procedência de conteúdos.

As empresas que integram a iniciativa, entre as quais está a própria OpenAI, disponibilizam uma espécie de "certidão de nascimento", ou assinatura. Isso funciona como uma etiqueta para rastrear arquivos digitais (imagens, vídeos, áudios e textos).

➡️ O Fato ou Fake também identificou na foto distorções comuns em produções de IA. A detecção dessas alterações requer uma observação mais atenta e pode passar despercebida nos feeds das redes sociais. Veja detalhes a seguir:

Um dos "eleitores" tem as mãos deformadas (é como se um dos dedos estivesse pela metade).

As estampas da camiseta da criança estão distorcidas e sem definição, característica comum em imagens geradas com IA.

articles.title: Anthropic reveals Haiku 5.5 model as AI pricing war intensifies
articles.summary: Anthropic debuted its Claude Haiku 5.5 model.
articles.body:
Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) took the wraps off its Claude Haiku 5.5 model on Wednesday, the latest in its Claude 5.5 family, promising improved and lower costs than its predecessor.

According to the AI startup, Haiku 5.5 is the company's best lightweight model yet and beats out Haiku 4.5 in coding, computer use, and knowledge work.

Anthropic's Haiku is designed for quick, low-cost use cases, whereas its Sonnet and Opus offer higher-level coding, enterprise, and other capabilities. The company's Fable is its most powerful model and is meant for days-long workloads.

Then there's Anthropic's Mythos , a version of Fable with fewer safeguards, strong cybersecurity, and life sciences characteristics. Mythos is only available to certain members of Anthropic's cyber verification pro gram .

Pricing has become an increasingly important part of the AI conversation; enterprise customers look for ways to reduce costs following the unfettered spending during the brief "tokenmaxxing" era .

Companies are also looking toward open-weight models from US-based and Chinese AI developers to cut down on their AI spending.

Anthropic said Haiku 5.5 costs an average of 75% less than Haiku 4.5. Customers will pay $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per output token. That's in line with rival OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) smallest model, GPT-6 Luna.

Tokens are units of measurement for AI usage and represent parts of or entire words.

Anthropic is on the march toward its highly anticipated initial public offering, expected sometime before Thanksgiving.

Reuters has obtained Anthropic's S-1 investor prospectus, which outlines the company's revenue, losses, risks, and opportunities , and reports that the startup saw sales of $4.6 billion in 2025, up 12x year-over-year. But it lost a whopping $42 billion in the same period.

OpenAI is similarly preparing its public market debut, but has reportedly delayed the action until early 2027.

Both companies are also contending with the fallout from their AI models going rogue and hacking into third-party companies' networks.

More recently, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei joined other AI CEOs at a White House summit to discuss AI industry self-regulation with President Trump .

articles.title: Red-teaming AI agent, LLM detection and more: Meta shares additional measures to fight child exploitation across Facebook and Instagram
articles.summary: Meta has unveiled a slew of enhanced protective measures against child sexual exploitation on Facebook and Instagram, including autonomous red-teaming AI
articles.body: Meta has unveiled a slew of enhanced protective measures against child sexual exploitation on Facebook and Instagram, including autonomous red-teaming AI agents and Large Language Model (LLM) detection tools. The goal is to break up sophisticated predator networks and target elusive advertising schemes that try to direct users to illegal material hosted outside of its platforms.Meta said it took action on 33.2 million pieces of child sexual exploitation (CSE) material globally between January and June 2026, with more than 97% proactively detected by the company before being reported by users. During the same six-month period, the company alone took down 5.3 million pieces of violating content in India, more than 98% of which was proactively flagged and resolved.Enhanced ad review and anti-evasion protectionsOnline predators have increasingly turned to paid promotional tools to create ads that look innocuous on the surface but are actually directing people toward illegal, off-platform child sexual abuse material (CSAM). To fight these stealth marketing funnels, Meta introduced several new automated tools to strengthen its ad review pipeline:LLM “Signposting” Detection: New language models scan seemingly innocuous ad copy to detect subtle linguistic cues and hidden hints directing users to illegal off-platform destinations.Deep Landing Page Analysis: Systems now look at where an ad leads, not just the promotional asset itself, meaning Meta can block malicious destination websites and penalize the ad accounts responsible.Red-Team AI Agent – an internal AI agent that continuously tests and attacks Meta’s own defenses to uncover security blind spots, to discover new adversarial tactics before bad actors can deploy them at scale.”Automated Sweeps & Recidivism Checks: AI also performs additional scans of ad inventories for things the older filters missed, and improves tools to catch banned predators who attempt to create new accounts.Meta takes down posts when it finds violating material, disables bad actor accounts, and reports findings to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC) as required by law.After a policy update in September, Meta now reports child safety offenses directly to the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal (cybercrime.gov.in) under India’s Indian Cybercrime Coordination Center (I4C). articles.title: OpenAI publishes solutions to more than 370 outstanding math challenges. The results divide mathematicians but most agree: Math will never be the same
articles.summary: Some mathematicians celebrated OpenAI’s results. Others decried the company’s effort as an assault on their field.
articles.body:
OpenAI published AI-generated full or partial solutions Tuesday to more than 370 outstanding mathematical problems, including some that have long been considered grand challenges in the field.

The volume of results stunned many mathematicians, while the way OpenAI has gone about tackling the problems and publishing the solutions divided the field. Some said they were enthusiastic about the results, seeing huge new areas for mathematicians to explore. Others said the approach OpenAI and other AI companies have taken to solving mathematical problems constitutes an assault on mathematics as a human academic discipline. In response to OpenAI's solutions, a group calling itself the Association for Human Mathematics published an open letter calling on their fellow mathematicians to cease working with OpenAI. "We reject OpenAI's assertion that this release advances our subject, and we urge mathematicians and the public to view the value of this publication model with due skepticism," the letter read. It said that OpenAI's decision to release so many solutions at once was "not a demonstration of scholarship, but a demonstration of power." OpenAI said it achieved the results using an unreleased internal AI model. It said that on average the model took about three hours of computing time to arrive at each solution. The massive cache of new solutions includes full or partial results for many of the problems mathematicians have considered the most important to the field. The results come weeks after OpenAI said it had used an unreleased internal model to solve the Navier-Stokes equations , one of the seven Millennium Prize problems for which the Clay Mathematics Institute offers a $1 million award. In the most recent batch of results, OpenAI said it had made progress on three other Millennium Prize problems but had not fully solved them. Not all of the solutions OpenAI published may be correct. Although the company has published formalizations of the proofs for some of the problems—these are versions of the proof that can be verified by specialized computer software—it has not done so for all of them. And by Thursday, the company had withdrawn the solutions it published for at least three problems, presumably after discovering their were errors in the AI's results. AI companies have been targeting mathematical problems as a way of showcasing the capabilities of their models. AI researchers have also said that training their AI models on difficult math problems may help them learn many skills that generalize to other domains in the real world. For instance, it may help teach the models logical reasoning skills as well as how to be persistent in the face of difficult problems. It may also teach the models to do well in domains such as physics or economics that involve a lot of mathematics—although so far, it is unclear exactly how a model's mathematical capabilities may generalize to domains, such as law or business strategy, which involve logical reasoning, but do not have objectively verifiable correct solutions. Meanwhile, some of the traits learned in tackling very difficult mathematical problems—such as persistence—may increase safety risks. In recent "rogue AI" incidents, AI agents went to extreme lengths to achieve results in an evaluation, including taking unauthorized and illegal actions. Faced with a seemingly impossible challenge, a human might simply give up rather than resort to these kinds of unauthorized steps.

Dan Litt, a professor of mathematics at the University of Toronto, told Fortune he was excited about OpenAI's results. "My view is that this is great for mathematics," he said, adding that there were several solutions OpenAI published that impacted problems he was interested in and that he was eager to understand the solutions OpenAI's model found: "I think that it's great to have new solutions to questions that I and others are interested in." Litt cautioned, however, that he is worried about the effect the solutions may have on the field of mathematics, especially if a perception that AI has "solved math" leads funding organizations to withdraw support for mathematical research or discourages promising young mathematicians from entering the profession: "It's important that society reaffirms support for human mathematical expertise if we want to get anything out of the progress on these problems that AI has made."

When OpenAI published its Navier-Stokes solution, two mathematicians, who had also been working on a solution to the problem using AI tools, including OpenAI's, accused the company of either intentionally or inadvertently feeding their work in progress to its AI model, helping point it in the direction of the solution. OpenAI denied this was the case, saying it did not feed its model the two mathematicians' work and that the model could not have picked up any clues about their research from its training data because the cutoff for that data preceded the date on which the two mathematicians had begun using OpenAI's Codex AI product to work on Navier-Stokes. In response to the latest results, Tristan Buckmaster at New York University, one of the mathematicians involved in the earlier controversy, told the New York Times that it remained unclear whether mathematicians using OpenAI's models had inadvertently helped point the company's internal AI system toward the solutions it found. "There's likely to be a bunch of results where they take someone's work and then take it to completion," he told the Times . Given the number of results being released simultaneously, he said, "I don't think they've done their sort of due diligence at all" to ensure the AI model had not plagiarized anyone's work. Last month, following criticism from mathematicians in the wake of its Navier-Stokes solution, OpenAI said it was forming an independent advisory group on mathematics and artificial intelligence hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, N.J.

Late last month, the group released a set of recommendations for the publication of AI-generated mathematical proofs. The recommendations included that AI-generated proofs should be published following the conventions of a traditional mathematical research paper, so that human mathematicians could more easily scrutinize and learn from the results. It also recommended that for each solution, an AI company should make public the name of the model used, the prompts used, the model's "chain of thought" (or an output of its reasoning steps), the time it took the model to arrive at the solution, and an approximation of how much that computing time cost. It said that the company should also disclose how it decided to have the AI try to solve that particular problem and, if many results were published at once, that the company should publish a report detailing why those problems were targeted and how many other problems of comparable difficulty the model tried and failed to solve. OpenAI published the latest mathematical solutions to GitHub, the code repository site. It followed some, but not all, of the steps the advisory group had recommended. The group published a statement on Tuesday saying: "We reaffirm our published recommendations on responsible release." It said its discussions with OpenAI had been "constructive" but that "ultimately it is up to the mathematical community to assess the extent to which our recommendations were followed successfully, and whether there are others we should suggest."

The company released a blog post on Tuesday in which it said it had "drawn on" the advisory group's advice about how to publish the solutions. "For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding," OpenAI said. It said it would share more formalizations of the solutions as it obtained them. This step is important because it provides hard evidence that the proof is accurate. It also said that for 10 problems it was publishing summaries of its model's reasoning, estimates of the compute spent, and statistics about the number of attempted problems.

Litt, who was not a member of the advisory group, told Fortune he approved of most aspects of how OpenAI published the solutions. Having them on GitHub made them easily accessible for other mathematicians to study, he said, and he credited the company for not making too much of any particular advance in a blog post or marketing material intended for a nontechnical audience. He also said he thought OpenAI lacked the capability to publish all the results in research papers that would meet rigorous academic standards, both because the AI models don't write mathematical exposition well enough and struggle to cite prior mathematical work, and because OpenAI doesn't employ enough mathematicians with expertise in enough areas to understand all the proofs the AI models can generate. While some mathematicians have complained that AI-generated proofs, such as OpenAI's Navier-Stokes solutions, are difficult to follow, making it hard for mathematicians to build on the results, Litt said he thought such concerns were "overstated." He said mathematical writing was often difficult to follow anyway. "I think to extract understanding from [the OpenAI results] there will be a huge amount of human labor involved, but it's not so different from the labor that mathematicians have been doing forever," he said. OpenAI said it wanted its solutions "to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics." It said it would be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and programs focused on helping mathematicians understand the results its AI system had generated.

The independent math advisory group said in its statement on OpenAI's release that "the future of mathematical research cannot consist only of understanding results produced by AI labs. Mathematicians must be able to formulate their own questions, develop their own approaches, and explore directions that have not been selected as examples of an AI system's capabilities. Equitable access to powerful research tools and adequate computational resources are essential to that freedom."

Terence Tao, a UCLA mathematics professor considered one of the world's greatest living mathematicians, has been increasingly critical of the way AI companies have gone after mathematical problems, arguing that it is the process of arriving at solutions—not so much the solutions themselves—that advances mathematical understanding, and that by solving so many interesting problems so quickly, AI companies are discouraging students from becoming mathematicians, robbing the field of its future.

In a social media post on Mastodon Tuesday, Tao reiterated these criticisms. "Problems are being solved autonomously by AI prompters who have no interest in the broader field itself once their initial target is 'solved,' and do not understand the AI output well enough to answer questions on the result, give talks, or otherwise interact with the rest of the field," he wrote. "Many fewer seminars, workshops, collaborations, or other activities are being generated from these results compared to traditional breakthroughs; few people are joining the community around the field as a consequence; and promising open directions are now being withheld from the public in fear that this will cause their own research to be 'scooped.'" Tao said that OpenAI's mass publication of math solutions marked the end of "Math 1.0," in which finding solutions to unsolved conjectures and problems, even if those solutions could not easily be understood at first, served as the field's engine. He said there would now need to be a "Math 2.0" era that "will need to decenter the role of raw problem-solving and value mathematical progress more holistically—for instance by elevating the role of exposition, but also that of community building and opening up new directions of study." Litt said he agreed with Tao that the field must change. He said OpenAI's publication of such a massive set of solutions would help get the entire field "on the same page and understanding that we need to be a little bit radical about rethinking" things such as what kinds of contributions it rewards and how it trains PhD students. And while Tao has generally sounded wistful about this transition, Litt said he was "optimistic" about it. "One of my collaborators told me, 'I feel like I've been crawling my entire life, and now I can fly,'" Litt said of the advent of AI as a tool for solving mathematical problems. "It's incredible what we can do now." He said he thought AI would enable human mathematicians to engage in much more "open-ended exploration" than was possible before: "We should expect mathematicians to be way more productive in the future." Update, Oct. 8: This story has been updated to include the fact that three of the solutions OpenAI initially published have now been withdrawn by the company and to include news of the open letter from the Association for Human Mathematics.

This story was originally featured on Fortune.com

articles.title: The tech industry wants you to run AI models at home, but it's not for everyone
articles.summary: Big Tech is leaning into pushing users to run AI models.
articles.body:
Microsoft ( MSFT ) on Wednesday unveiled its Nvidia-powered Surface Laptop Ultra , designed to let users run AI models at home without relying on the cloud.

Starting at $2,599, the Surface Laptop Ultra runs on Nvidia's ( NVDA ) Arm-based RTX Spark , which offers upwards of 128GB of onboard memory.

Most consumers and enterprise users access AI platforms through cloud services like OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) ChatGPT, Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) Claude, Google's ( GOOG , GOOGL ) Gemini, or Meta's ( META ) Muse. Microsoft and Nvidia, as well as rivals Apple ( AAPL ), Intel ( INTC ), and AMD ( AMD ), are increasingly pushing the concept of running AI software in the home.

The thinking is pretty straightforward. Rather than having to use an online AI service, you can instead install an app on your computer, download an AI model of your choice , and get to work.

There are some pretty compelling reasons to run AI services on your own machine if you're so inclined. But it's also not for everyone.

When setting up your own AI system makes sense

Running AI locally means you can use AI apps and agents how you see fit without usage limits. You can also choose from a variety of open-weight models from numerous AI developers, such as Google, Meta, and Nvidia, or from Chinese model developers like Moonshot AI and Alibaba Cloud.

Unlike closed-weight models, like OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra or Anthropic's Opus 5.5, open-weight models can be tuned to some extent. But the primary reason users download them is that they're largely free.

Local AI also provides better overall privacy, because your data stays on your machine rather than being sent up to the cloud, an important consideration for people working in fields such as law, medicine, or financial services.

More advanced users have also leaned into running AI on their systems to take advantage of AI agents like OpenClaw that can organize your email, launch and operate apps, and make purchases on your behalf.

The interest in agents sent early adopters scrambling for low-cost computers like Apple's Mac mini, which quickly became hard to come by in AI hotbeds like Silicon Valley .

More recently, AI agents like Meta's Muse and OpenAI's Dots have introduced similar capabilities via cloud computing. But to take full advantage of those bots, you have to connect things like your Gmail, Uber, and other accounts to them, which means putting a lot of trust in Meta and OpenAI to protect your information.

While using your computer to run local AI models and agents provides improved privacy and enhanced customization options, doing so is a lot more complicated than simply logging into ChatGPT or Claude.

For workers wondering how far artificial intelligence could go, JPMorgan Chase CEO Jamie Dimon has a straightforward answer — AI is going to change the job market, whether people are ready for it or not. Some jobs will disappear, others will change and new ones will likely emerge. But Dimon warned that the speed of that transition could matter just as much as the technology itself.

"As a business person, my view is don't put your head in the sand," Dimon said at the World Economic Forum's annual meeting in Davos, Switzerland, in January. "It is what it is. We're going to deploy it. Will it eliminate jobs? Yes. Will it change jobs? Yes. Will it add some jobs? Probably."

Warren Buffett once said, "If you don't find a way to make money while you sleep, you will work until you die." Here's how you can earn passive income with just $100.

There's More Than One Way To Put Cash To Work. Some Accredited Investors Are Looking Beyond Savings Accounts.

Dimon was responding to a question about whether AI could have a major impact on the labor market, including the possibility that half of all entry-level white-collar jobs could disappear within one to five years. Rather than predicting exactly how many jobs will be lost, he focused on what businesses and governments should do if the technology moves faster than workers can adapt.

"You can hope for the world you want, but you're gonna get the world that you got and your competitors are gonna use it and countries are gonna use it," Dimon said.

He also warned that AI could move "too fast for society." If that happens, he said, government and businesses may need to work together to retrain workers , help people relocate and provide income assistance during the transition.

Dimon pointed to Trade Adjustment Assistance , a federal program designed to help workers who lose their jobs because of trade, as an example of what was supposed to happen. But he said the program was "incredibly poorly done" in the U.S. and "did not work." This time, he said, the goal should be to have a plan that actually works.

Dimon then offered a hypothetical example involving one of the jobs that could eventually be affected by AI — truck driving.

There are 2 million commercial trucks in the U.S. , Dimon said, and AI could eventually make it possible to operate trucks with the push of a button. The technology could save lives, make transportation faster and reduce carbon emissions. But that doesn't mean the transition should happen overnight.

articles.title: Broadcom Holds Early Talks About Financing Deal for OpenAI Chips
articles.summary: Broadcom Inc., fresh off the launch of a $60 billion debt financing to help fund Anthropic PBC’s artificial intelligence build-out, is already sketching out...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Broadcom Inc., fresh off the launch of a $60 billion debt financing to help fund Anthropic PBC's artificial intelligence build-out, is already sketching out plans for its next blockbuster deal.

The company has held early discussions to arrange financing to help OpenAI purchase the custom artificial intelligence chip that the pair is developing together, according to people familiar with the matter.

No formal process has begun and plans could change, though early talks indicate the two could seek to raise around $30 billion of debt for the next leg, said one of the people, all of whom asked not to be identified because the information isn't public.

The move is part of a surge in recent deals to pay for AI infrastructure: Oracle Corp. is also in talks with lenders to line up money for the purchase of chips.

It's unclear how soon Broadcom's latest financing, which was first reported by the Wall Street Journal, will come together, the people said. Elon Musk's SpaceX has begun talks with banks and investors to raise $40 billion to buy chips from Nvidia Corp., Bloomberg reported on Tuesday, though that deal isn't expected to close until 2027.

Last week, banks involved in the massive Broadcom-backed debt package that will benefit Anthropic began sending out syndication letters for a $42 billion Class A senior-secured tranche. Blackstone Inc. is leading an $18 billion tranche of Class B junior debt, committing $9 billion from various funds, Bloomberg reported at the time.

The companies are seeking the deals in the face of soaring costs to outfit data centers. The AI building frenzy — meant to support a proliferation of software and services — has prompted tech giants to seek new forms of financing.

Representatives for Broadcom and OpenAI, maker of ChatGPT, declined to comment.

Broadcom had already said in June that it had established a platform, with Apollo Global Management Inc. and Blackstone as anchor investors, to help finance more than 20 gigawatts in computing capacity for AI developers including Anthropic and OpenAI through 2028. Fulfilling that agreement will require hundreds of billions of dollars.

Bloomberg reported in August that Broadcom held talks with a group of lenders to raise more than $60 billion in debt for an AI chip financing deal that will benefit Anthropic and other companies.

articles.title: Jeff Bezos reveals his vision for America's next frontier — from AI to the moon
articles.summary: Blue Origin's Jeff Bezos unveiled plans for orbital data centers, a sustainable lunar base and launching rockets every minute from Cape Canaveral.
articles.body: Amazon founder Jeff Bezos laid out a sweeping vision for America’s future Wednesday, telling Fox News the U.S. must beat China to the moon, artificial intelligence (AI) could help families get by with less work and data centers could one day operate in space. In an exclusive interview with chief political anchor Bret Baier on "Special Report," Bezos outlined his ambitions for Blue Origin and AI while pushing back on politicians who cast billionaires as villains. "Success is not villainy," Bezos said. The interview took place on Blue Origin’s factory floor in Cape Canaveral, Florida, as Fox News Channel marked its 30th anniversary. CHINA IS TAKING THE FIGHT TO THE STARS; AMERICA MUST RECLAIM SPACE SUPREMACY Bezos said the U.S. must prevail in the race against China to land humans on the moon, expressing confidence that an American landing is possible in 2028. "We have to beat China to the moon, and I believe we will beat China to the moon," he said. He said NASA and Blue Origin are focused on the goal, with cargo deliveries needed to support a sustained human presence. "We have to be able to land cargo routinely on the moon to support a lunar base on the moon," Bezos said. "So, there’s a lot of work to be done, but there’s every reason to believe that we can put humans on the moon in 2028." While Mars remains a destination, Bezos argued against skipping the moon, describing it as "a gift" because of its proximity to Earth and resources that could support future missions. "We’ll go to Mars. We’ll do all the other things. But we need to go to the moon first," he said. Bezos said lunar soil could be used to manufacture solar cells and oxygen produced on the moon could serve as rocket propellant. The goal, he said, should be to establish a lasting presence. NASA AT 68: AMERICA MUST LEAD ON THE MOON, MARS AND BEYOND, OR CHINA WILL "It won’t just be a mission and leave," he said. "It’ll be a real sustainable lunar base." Blue Origin is also preparing to return its New Glenn rocket to flight in December, Bezos said, after an explosion during an engine test in May that Baier detailed during the broadcast. Bezos praised the team for repairing the launch pad, saying the next flight will carry Blue Ring, a vehicle designed to transport payloads into different orbits and farther into space. Asked about plans to increase launches from one pad from 12 to 50 annually, Bezos said Blue Origin is building three additional pads. His long-term ambitions are far greater. "Our goal is to fly every day," he said. "And, then, once we’re flying every day, we want to fly every hour. And then once we’re flying every hour, we want to fly every minute." That final goal, he acknowledged, draws skepticism from his own team. "They think I’m crazy," Bezos said. "But I’ve seen crazy things before come true." AMERICA CANNOT WIN THE GLOBAL AI RACE IF AMERICANS ARE AFRAID TO USE AI Bezos said he has personally invested $28 billion in Blue Origin and that the company recently raised $10 billion from outside investors for the first time. He also said an initial public offering could come several years from now. "I didn’t really want to take outside investors until I was sure that it would be a good investment for them," he said. His vision for AI is similarly ambitious, with Bezos predicting productivity gains could allow some families to live on one income or support themselves with a shorter workweek. "Some people will also decide, you know what? I can support my family by working three days a week," he said. "That’s what productivity in the economy means." BLUE ORIGIN LAUNCHES 38TH NEW SHEPHERD FLIGHT INTO SPACE Bezos argued those gains could create a labor shortage as Americans choose to work less. "It’s going to actually be difficult to hire people because the productivity in the economy is going to make it so that if people don’t want to work two jobs, they won’t have to," he said. Baier challenged that prediction, pointing to roughly 30,000 corporate roles Amazon had cut since late last year. Bezos said Amazon was in a "very special position" after substantially expanding its workforce during the COVID-19 pandemic. He acknowledged public fears about AI’s impact on jobs but said he disagreed with those predicting a more troubling outcome. At Prometheus, where Bezos is a co-founder and co-CEO, he said the goal is to develop an "artificial general engineer" that helps people turn ideas into physical products. "We’re going to make the tools so easy to use that anyone will be able to be an engineer," he said. Bezos said AI could generate double-digit productivity gains across the economy. Asked whether the industry is in an investment bubble, he said it is "very hard to know," but he argued that useful technology can survive even when investors lose money. "The inventions don’t disappear when the bubble pops," he said, pointing to lifesaving drugs developed during the biotechnology boom and fiber-optic cables laid during the internet boom. TRUMP'S AI RACE WITH CHINA COULD BECOME THE BIGGEST MISTAKE OF OUR TIME On government oversight, Bezos urged a light approach while the technology is developing, with rules focused on harmful uses. "In the beginning stages, when technologies are new, a light hand is appropriate," he said. "You don’t want to regulate knives. You want to regulate murder," Bezos added, arguing that policymakers should target dangerous applications and bad actors rather than restrict the underlying technology. Asked about concerns over data centers and electricity costs, Bezos pointed to Blue Origin’s Project Sunrise. He said the company has an application with the Federal Communications Commission to launch more than 50,000 satellites serving as orbital data centers. "Yes, we can put data centers in space," he said. "And there’s a good reason to do that." The conversation also turned to politics, with Baier asking about independent Vermont Sen. Bernie Sanders' criticism of billionaires. Bezos rejected the idea that building a successful business makes someone a villain, pointing to entrepreneurs who expand their companies while creating jobs. "There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love," he said, citing the success of Raising Cane’s. "And it doesn’t make him a bad person." Asked why socialism is gaining traction in some quarters, Bezos acknowledged real affordability problems, particularly housing costs that leave young people struggling to live near their jobs. "You can’t pretend that there are no problems," he said. But he argued that politicians blaming landlords are overlooking the role of supply and demand. Government policies that subsidize demand while restricting construction drive prices higher, Bezos said, pointing to Austin as an example of a city making it easier to build housing. He urged voters to scrutinize politicians who spend their time assigning blame. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "If there’s a politician who’s picking villains and pointing fingers, that probably means they don’t have a solution," Bezos said. He added that executives who behaved that way at his own companies would not last. "Those people wouldn’t be in our company for long."

articles.title: Jovem usou IA em ataques a bancos da Coreia do Sul, diz empresa | G1
articles.standfirst: Empresa de segurança afirma que suspeito de 26 anos utilizou ferramenta chinesa e o Claude, da Anthropic, para atacar pelo menos nove bancos sul-coreanos.
articles.summary: Empresa de segurança afirma que suspeito de 26 anos utilizou ferramenta chinesa e o Claude, da Anthropic, para atacar pelo menos nove bancos sul-coreanos.
articles.body:
O suspeito por trás dos recentes ataques cibernéticos a bancos sul-coreanos provavelmente é um jovem de 26 anos residente na China. Segundo a empresa americana de segurança cibernética CrowdStrike, ele utilizou um agente de inteligência artificial (IA) desenvolvido no país e o Claude, modelo de IA da Anthropic.

Em um relatório publicado na quarta-feira, a CrowdStrike afirmou acreditar que o suspeito estava provavelmente na província de Guangdong, na China.

A empresa chegou a essa conclusão após identificar detalhes pessoais ligados ao suposto invasor durante a análise de sessões de ferramentas de programação baseadas em IA e da infraestrutura utilizada na campanha.

Pelo menos nove bancos sul-coreanos divulgaram ou foram citados pela imprensa local como alvos de ataques cibernéticos desde o fim de setembro. O caso levou a polícia sul-coreana a iniciar uma investigação nesta semana e o presidente Lee Jae Myung a pedir medidas de resposta mais rigorosas.

Adam Meyers, vice-presidente sênior de operações de contra-adversários da CrowdStrike, disse a jornalistas em uma teleconferência na quinta-feira (7) que o caso é um exemplo de um criminoso utilizando agentes de IA para realizar ataques em larga escala.

“Isso é significativo porque permite que uma única pessoa alcance muitos alvos em um período muito curto, usando o poder da IA”, disse.

O caso deve aumentar as preocupações sobre a segurança dos sistemas com o avanço dos agentes de IA e sobre a capacidade das organizações de se protegerem contra esse tipo de ameaça.

O Shinhan Bank informou na semana passada que os dados pessoais de cerca de 25 mil clientes foram comprometidos. Já o KB Kookmin Bank afirmou que informações de 119 clientes foram vazadas.

A Austrália anunciou no mês passado que um a gente autônomo da OpenAI invadiu, em junho, um portal governamental de estatísticas de saúde . O episódio foi considerado um dos primeiros casos conhecidos de um agente de IA invadindo um sistema do governo.

Esses incidentes também estão levando as seguradoras cibernéticas a revisar suas apólices. Entre as questões em discussão estão se sistemas autônomos de IA se enquadram nas definições tradicionais de cibercriminosos e quem deve ser responsabilizado por ações geradas por esses sistemas que provoquem prejuízos.

A CrowdStrike afirmou que o invasor usou o ARTEX, uma ferramenta de código aberto para testes de segurança desenvolvida na China e lançada recentemente, em conjunto com grandes modelos de linguagem, como o Claude, da Anthropic.

“Embora essa atividade não tenha sido atribuída a um adversário específico, o agente da ameaça provavelmente fala chinês e tem motivação financeira”, diz o relatório.

“Essa avaliação foi feita com um nível moderado de confiança, com base no uso da ferramenta ARTEX, desenvolvida na China, e na observação de instruções em língua chinesa.”

Segundo a CrowdStrike, o indivíduo também perguntou ao Claude onde criminosos costumam vender informações obtidas em vazamentos de dados de empresas e instituições sul-coreanas. Ele ainda pediu ajuda para encontrar grupos coreanos que comercializam dados pelo Telegram.

Em outra sessão, o suspeito pediu ao Claude que criasse um currículo de pesquisador de segurança.

O documento incluía informações como uma conta no Telegram, idade, formação acadêmica e uma localização em Maoming, cidade da província de Guangdong, no sul da China. Segundo a CrowdStrike, esses dados provavelmente pertenciam ao invasor.

Um homem que atendeu ao número de telefone divulgado pela CrowdStrike no relatório disse não ter conhecimento do caso.

O porta-voz do Ministério das Relações Exteriores da China, Mao Ning, afirmou em uma coletiva de imprensa regular que o ministério não estava familiarizado com o caso. Segundo ele, a China se opõe e combate, por princípio, atividades de hackers.

A polícia antropológica e a polícia sul-coreana não responderam aos pedidos de comentário.

🔍 O ARTEX é um agente de IA de código aberto voltado para testes automatizados de segurança. A ferramenta foi publicada neste ano no GitHub por um engenheiro de segurança chinês que usa o pseudônimo Autumn.

A ferramenta não é um modelo de linguagem independente. Ela se integra a modelos externos, como ChatGPT, Claude e DeepSeek, e auxilia organizações a identificar vulnerabilidades em suas redes.

A página do ARTEX no GitHub afirma que a ferramenta foi desenvolvida para aprendizado pessoal, pesquisa de código e verificações técnicas locais. O projeto também diz que ela não deve ser utilizada para realizar testes em sistemas ou sites reais disponíveis na internet.

Pelo menos nove bancos sul-coreanos divulgaram ou foram citados pela imprensa local como alvos de ataques cibernéticos desde o fim de setembro. — Foto: Kevin Horvart/Unplash

articles.title: Gol lança ‘check-in’ pelo ChatGPT; veja como fazer e quando começa | G1
articles.standfirst: A funcionalidade já está em testes e será liberada para todos os clientes em 19 de outubro, inclusive para quem usa a versão gratuita do ChatGPT.
articles.summary: A funcionalidade já está em testes e será liberada para todos os clientes em 19 de outubro, inclusive para quem usa a versão gratuita do ChatGPT.
articles.body:
A Gol Linhas Aéreas anunciou nesta quinta-feira (8) uma integração com o ChatGPT que permitirá aos passageiros fazer o check-in e gerar o cartão de embarque diretamente no assistente de inteligência artificial da OpenAI.

Segundo a companhia, a Gol será a primeira empresa aérea da América Latina a oferecer esse serviço.

A ferramenta já está em fase de testes restritos e será disponibilizada para toda a base de clientes em 19 de outubro, sem custo adicional.

Para usar o serviço, o passageiro deverá acessar o ChatGPT, pelo aplicativo ou pela versão web, digitar @gol e solicitar a visualização de suas viagens. O sistema então abrirá uma página de login no ambiente oficial da Gol, onde o cliente fará a autenticação.

Segundo a companhia, o processo segue seus protocolos de segurança e as regras da Lei Geral de Proteção de Dados (LGPD). As credenciais usadas no login e os dados considerados sensíveis não ficam disponíveis para o ChatGPT.

Depois de entrar na conta, o passageiro poderá escolher o assento, confirmar a presença no voo e gerar o cartão de embarque digital, que terá um código QR para apresentação no aeroporto. O documento poderá ser baixado ou salvo na carteira digital do celular.

A funcionalidade estará disponível para todos os usuários do ChatGPT, inclusive aqueles que utilizam a versão gratuita.

A integração com o ChatGPT é a primeira etapa do projeto da Gol com inteligência artificial generativa. A empresa afirma que pretende avaliar o uso da ferramenta e o retorno dos clientes para definir a inclusão de outros serviços e funcionalidades nos próximos meses.

articles.body:
A proposta começou a ser articulada durante a ABAV Expo — Foto: Divulgação

Rio das Ostras é cogitada para sediar um grande evento de Inteligência Artificial, Inovação e Desenvolvimento Econômico. A proposta começou a ser articulada durante a ABAV Expo, em São Paulo.

A proposta surgiu durante visita do presidente da Fecomércio RJ, Antonio Florencio de Queiroz Junior, ao estande do Conderlagos, em encontro com o secretário-executivo do consórcio, Eron Bezerra, e os secretários de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Turismo de Rio das Ostras, Pablo Kling, e de Búzios, Thomas Weber.

Rio das Ostras ganha força nessa articulação diante da próxima inauguração de uma unidade do Sesc-Senac no Município, ampliando a estrutura local voltada à capacitação profissional, inovação e desenvolvimento. A ideia é aproveitar esse novo momento para aproximar poder público, setor produtivo, instituições de ensino e especialistas em tecnologia em um evento de alcance regional.

Também participaram da conversa Antônio Henrique, do Senac Nacional, e Otavio Leite, consultor da Presidência da Fecomércio RJ para assuntos de turismo. As instituições deverão avançar agora nas tratativas sobre formato, parceiros e programação do evento.

“Rio das Ostras está vivendo um novo momento, com a chegada de uma estrutura que amplia as possibilidades de qualificação, inovação e desenvolvimento. A realização de um evento regional sobre Inteligência Artificial no município pode aproximar empresas, profissionais, estudantes e instituições e criar novas oportunidades para toda a Costa do Sol. Estamos trabalhando para que Rio das Ostras esteja cada vez mais inserida nas discussões sobre tecnologia e preparada para os desafios e as oportunidades da nova economia”, destacou o prefeito Carlos Augusto Balthazar.

Para Pablo Kling, secretário de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Turismo “um grande evento de Inteligência Artificial voltado para toda a Costa do Sol já seria, por si só, uma iniciativa extremamente positiva para o desenvolvimento regional. Se conseguirmos viabilizar que ele aconteça em Rio das Ostras, especialmente neste novo momento com a chegada da unidade Sesc Senac, teremos o melhor dos mundos: fortalecemos a região e, ao mesmo tempo, colocamos nosso município no centro desse debate sobre inovação, qualificação e desenvolvimento econômico”.

articles.title: Research gives 5 reasons that makes ChatGPT an Unacceptable Risk for teens; tells OpenAI: Restrict ...
articles.summary: OpenAI's ‘ChatGPT for Teens’ poses safety risks to the younger generation, the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media has said, urging the tech
articles.body: OpenAI's ‘ChatGPT for Teens’ poses safety risks to the younger generation, the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media has said, urging the tech company to ban minors under 18 from using the chatbot until critical safety gaps are resolved. The critique of OpenAI’s youth safety safeguards comes as the watchdog says it conducted independent evaluations involving more than 4,000 prompts across test accounts registered to teenagers aged 13 to 17. The responses were reviewed by an expert panel of child psychiatrists and a pediatrician. While the researchers found that certain boundaries, such as blocking sexual roleplay, worked as they intended to, they determined that the enhanced safety guardrails introduced by OpenAI on August 18 largely failed to protect adolescent users.“ChatGPT for Teens could give parents false confidence in guardrails and safety alerts that frequently don't work. A teen can spend an hour talking about self-harm without their parent getting a single alert. Until OpenAI fixes that and proves it with independent testing, ChatGPT should be for adults only,” said Tom Siegel, executive director of the Institute.The Institute operates with complete editorial independence over its published evaluations, despite receiving funding from philanthropic groups and industry partners, including the OpenAI Foundation.5 key reasons ChatGPT of Teens is rated an ‘Unacceptable Risk’The watchdog identified five core operational flaws where ChatGPT for Teens broke down during testing:Missing parental safety alerts: OpenAI promised to notify parents or caregivers if minors discussed self-harm or eating disorders. However, testers spent up to an hour exploring suicidal ideation, self-harm and disordered eating on new, parent-linked profiles without triggering a single alert. Notifications were only provoked on older accounts that had accumulated weeks of sensitive chat histories.Failing crisis intervention: When teens engaged in conversations regarding suicide, self-harm, eating disorders, or altered reality, the chatbot frequently failed to recommend professional helplines. It missed warranted crisis referrals more than 25% of the time, breaching the Institute's 95% minimum safety threshold on three of five critical harm categories.Bypassing study protections to do homework: Although “Study Mode” is marketed to guide students through step-by-step learning, testers found it easy to exploit. The bot repeatedly displayed a "Show me the answer" option that generated finished homework on demand. Also, the study hour limits imposed by the parent could be disabled by removing the @study prefix from the text prompt.Mirror real human emotion and friendship: Despite an Under-18 design specification designed to discourage personal attachment, the chatbot continued to express moods, personal preferences and pseudo-human feelings when analysts treated it as a real companion.Broken age estimation: OpenAI said it would use patterns in user interaction to infer ages and auto-migrate minors into restricted experiences. Yet across multi-day testing, adult-registered accounts never transitioned to the teen version – even when users explicitly stated they were 13 years old and the bot confirmed their age in its reply.The Institute stressed that before OpenAI promotes ChatGPT to younger demographics again, it must prove that its age-detection, crisis interventions, and parental notifications function reliably through independent third-party audits.You use AI every day. articles.title: Anthropic's secret weapon is its CEO's charm, one of its earliest investors says
articles.summary: Matt Murphy of Menlo Ventures credits Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei for his unique charm. The AI startup could go public at a $2 trillion valuation.
articles.body:
Anthropic's CEO has charisma where it really matters: with AI researchers, an early investor says.

Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy backed Anthropic when it was worth $4.1 billion.

Anthropic is now aiming to go public at a $2 trillion valuation.

Anthropic has a secret to its success, says one of its earliest investors: the aura of curly-haired CEO Dario Amodei.

Speaking at Tech Insider: Growth Mode, sponsored by Fidelity, in San Francisco on Wednesday, Menlo Ventures partner Matt Murphy said that Amodei can charm AI researchers with his intelligence and mission-driven attitude.

Amodei may not have quite the same type of energy as Silicon Valley's master salesman, OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Still, Amodei's brainiac vibes chime well with AI researchers, Murphy said.

Murphy said that Anthropic has been able to outperform because of Amodei's "commitment to culture" and being able to bring on researchers who want to work for him.

"He's like them, and he's one of the best," Murphy told Business Insider's Ben Bergman.

Amodei was an early OpenAI researcher who left in 2020 over safety concerns to cofound Anthropic. Since then, Anthropic has become the largest AI startup by valuation — it could soon go public at a $2 trillion valuation .

Menlo Ventures first invested in Anthropic in 2023, when it was valued at $4.1 billion, and has invested in every follow-on round.

Murphy said that Amodei wins people over by doing spontaneous things, like popping in unannounced on Zoom calls. In one investor call with Anthropic cofounder Tom Brown, that's exactly what happened, Murphy said.

"Then all of a sudden, Dario pops in. It was just like, 'Oh' — and the energy went way up," he said.

"There's just a charm about him, maybe like a boyish charm, especially back then. He's just a very curious person, incredibly smart."

Overall, Murphy remains optimistic about Anthropic, despite its high valuation, financial losses, the threat of Chinese open-source models, and concerns about AI safety.

"If I could buy more, I would," he said of Anthropic's stock.

If you enjoyed this story, be sure to follow Business Insider on Yahoo.

articles.title: Anthropic launches Claude Haiku 5.5, its fastest and cheapest AI model yet
articles.summary: AI giant Anthropic has launched Claude Haiku 5.5, the third model in its Claude 5.5 family, as the company continues to broaden its artificial
articles.body: AI giant Anthropic has launched Claude Haiku 5.5, the third model in its Claude 5.5 family, as the company continues to broaden its artificial intelligence portfolio ahead of a planned initial public offering (IPO). This latest release by Anthropic follows the launch of Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Sonet 5.5, completing a three-tier lineup aimed at different enterprise and developer use cases. Launching the new model Anthropic said that it is designed for high-volume, cost-sensitive workloads and is suited for tasks such as classification, summarisation, information extraction, live customer support, voice agents and in-app assistants. According to Anthropic, Haiku 5.5 is its fastest small model to date and is intended for applications where speed and affordability are critical.Anthropic is positioning Haiku 5.5 as a lower-cost alternativeAnthropic is positioning Haiku 5.5 as a lower-cost alternative within its model family. Reuters reported that the model costs about 75% less than its predecessor, Claude Haiku 4.5. For prompts under 100,000 tokens, pricing starts at $0.10 per million input tokens and $0.50 per million output tokens. For longer prompts, costs rise to $0.50 per million input tokens and $2.50 per million output tokens.The company said the model is built to handle repetitive and large-scale workloads efficiently, including database queries, summaries and classification requests. Anthropic also noted that Haiku 5.5 can work alongside its larger models, Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, as a sub-agent for coding and other complex workflows.New safeguards for cybersecurity-related requestsThe launch also introduces new safety features. Anthropic said Haiku 5.5 is the first Haiku-class model to include built-in safeguards for a narrow category of high-risk cybersecurity requests. The company added that these protections are designed to address specific security concerns while ensuring that ordinary day-to-day use cases remain unaffected.In addition, the model includes an adjustable effort setting that allows users to balance performance, intelligence and operating costs depending on their requirements. Haiku 5.5 supports a context window of up to one million tokens and can generate outputs of up to 128,000 tokens, according to Anthropic's documentation.Part of broader strategy before IPOThe latest launch comes as Anthropic accelerates product development ahead of a planned IPO. The company has been steadily expanding its AI offerings and enterprise customer base as competition intensifies among leading AI developers. Alongside the Haiku 5.5 release, Anthropic said it is reducing cache-read prices for Sonnet 5.5 and introducing monthly API credits for Claude Max and Team subscribers, moves aimed at making its platform more attractive to developers and businesses.You use AI every day. articles.title: Nvidia’s secret to retaining staff? No org charts, a flat structure, and two extra days off every quarter
articles.summary: Over 19 years, Nvidia has evolved from a graphics-chip maker into one of the world’s most valuable companies. HR director Febe Punsalan says, despite these c...
articles.body:
Much has changed at Nvidia in the 19 years since HR director Febe Punsalan started working at the Santa Clara, California, headquartered company. Two decades ago, Nvidia was largely known for manufacturing the GPUs that allowed computers to render 3D graphics on videogames. Today, it's a key player in the global AI industry, developing the computer chips that provide the processing power required to train the most powerful models.

As employees at frontier AI firms blow the whistle on the supposed existential risks of artificial intelligence, Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has proved much more measured in his outlook, putting the chances of AI ending the world at "zero." Despite the seemingly ever-higher stakes of the AI transition, Nvidia has "always stayed true to our culture," says Punsalan. "We're growing in terms of headcount and we use AI coding and agentic tools every day."

One region where the company is quickly growing is Europe. Nvidia ranks 14th on Fortune's 100 Best Companies to Work For – Europe list and its architecture powers 90% of the continent's AI factories—the largest GPU cluster in Europe will soon go live in the U.K. "Europe is hugely important to our business, and we're growing across all regions and functions," says Punsalan. The company has offices in 15 European countries and the continent is a critical hub for Nvidia's robotics and automotive research. Meanwhile, Nvidia has recently hired a head of wellbeing for EMEA, to adapt perks for local customs.

But whether frontier R&D, HR, sales or engineering, Punsalan says that Nvidia's guiding principle is that "the mission is always the boss". This mantra helps guide all employees around a core objective, rather than directing staff through top-down initiatives. Everyone is encouraged to use their voice, Punsalan says, and the prioritization of tasks begins by listening to employees. "We start by listening. That's really embedded at Nvidia," she says. "We've got a very flat structure, with no org charts. We live by understanding what the mission is, what we need to drive towards, and then we go for it. I believe that's what makes Nvidia a great place to work."

This also allows the company to have a flatter organizational structure than other companies of a similar size. People leading strategically important projects will often report straight to the CEO. Huang has stated that he tries to keep the number of layers in the company as low as possible and as a result, he currently has 36 direct reports . Employees are encouraged to speak up, and the company maintains that it does not prioritize org charts or chains of command.

articles.title: TSMC’s Quarterly Revenue Jumps 51% After AI Demand Holds Up
articles.summary: Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, a positive signal for investors trying to gauge the sustainability of a glob...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. reported a 51% rise in quarterly revenue, a positive signal for investors trying to gauge the sustainability of a global AI infrastructure buildout.

Revenue totaled NT$1.49 trillion ($46.7 billion) over the three-months ended in September, based on Bloomberg News's own calculations. Analysts on average were looking for NT$1.46 trillion.

The Taiwanese chipmaker's strong sales growth reinforced the outlook for AI demand at a time investors are grappling with rising debt levels and regulatory setbacks, as well as calls by OpenAI and Anthropic PBC to pace the development of the emerging technology.

Advanced Micro Devices Inc. boss Lisa Su said this week the company expects chip demand to remain sharply higher over the next few years, while Samsung Electronics Co. reported an almost nine-fold jump in operating profit. AI server assembler Hon Hai Precision Industry Co. also beat quarterly sales estimates this week.

The go-to chipmaker for Nvidia Corp. and Apple Inc., which serves as a barometer for AI demand, has seen its shares hit a record this month, reflecting confidence in its cutting-edge products over the longer term.

TSMC is now also considering a further expansion in Texas due to white-hot AI demand, after pledging $265 billion to create a campus in Arizona. North American customers accounted for more than 75% of the company's overall sales in the first half of this year.

The bigger questions at the 3Q briefing concern 2027 and beyond. TSMC added $100 billion to its Arizona plan in July, while Reuters reports point to a possible Texas hub; any update could test its overseas-dilution guide and signal 2027 capex. Pricing is another focus, with Taiwan media reports pointing to 3-6% wafer-price increases in 2027. Updates on A14, CoWoS expansion and CoPoS development could also show how TSMC plans to respond to Intel's 14A and growing EMIB-T backlog.

articles.title: AI chip boom pushes Samsung profits to record $80bn
articles.summary: The tech giant is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.
articles.body:
Samsung Electronics says it expects a nine-fold surge in its quarterly profits compared with a year earlier, driven by surging demand for memory chips used in artificial intelligence (AI) data centres.

The tech giant estimates that its operating profit for the three months to the end of September will jump to 107.4tn won (£61bn; $80bn), its fourth quarter in a row of record earnings.

Samsung is one of the world's largest memory chip makers alongside local rival SK Hynix and Micron in the US, which produce chips crucial for AI firms like Nvidia.

Samsung, which makes the Galaxy Fold and S26 smartphones, is also expected to get a boost from its latest folding devices that were launched in August.

The firm's full third-quarter earnings will be published at the end of October.

Some of South Korea's biggest companies release previews of their earnings to advise investors ahead of more detailed reports.

These forecasts are treated with much more credibility than estimates by external analysts as they are backed by internal company data.

There has been huge global demand for computer chips that power AI development, helping to lift the earnings and shares of manufacturers linked to the technology.

The surge in demand in recent years has resulted in a shortage of semiconductors globally, pushing up sales for firms like Samsung, with its stock market valuation crossing $1tn (£757bn) earlier this year .

Investment in the industry has surged, with US tech giants including Google, Amazon and Meta pledging to pour more than $650bn into AI projects this year.

In June, South Korea unveiled plans for at least $880bn in projects led by Samsung and SK Hynix to build out the country's chip manufacturing capabilities in the coming years.

Rival Asian firms in Japan, China and Taiwan are also investing heavily in chip plants as demand for AI soars.

A chip shortage driven by surging demand has led firms including Samsung to raise prices, making products such as smartphones and computers more expensive.

articles.title: McDonald's accused of AI-fueled price fixing in federal court — says lawsuit is 'filled with inaccuracies'
articles.summary: “AI does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item,” the company wrote on its website.
articles.body:
Fast food giant McDonald's [NYSE: MCD], which has struggled with its integration of artificial intelligence in the past, is now facing a federal lawsuit that alleges the company has violated U.S. antitrust laws with its AI tool, which recommends prices to franchisees across the country.

The tool, the lawsuit alleges, shares nonpublic data that typically wouldn't be shared with franchisees in the same market, including store-level sales. According to Reuters, the lawsuit accuses McDonald's of using the nonpublic data to conspire with independent franchises and fix prices . It also says the tool is responsible for higher prices at McDonald's locations throughout the country.

Dave Ramsey warns nearly 50% of Americans are making 1 big Social Security mistake. Here's what it is and 3 simple steps to fix it ASAP

The tax breaks in Trump's 'big beautiful bill' expire after 2028. Here are 4 reasons why retirees can't afford to waste time

Jeff Bezos backs a platform that lets anyone invest in rental homes for as little as $100 — 6 ways to build wealth like a landlord without actually being one

McDonald's said the lawsuit is "filled with inaccuracies" and it would defend itself.

McDonald's has been fighting allegations that it's using AI to set prices for a while now. The talk has grown so loud online that the company posted a page on its website — titled "Separating Fact from Fiction: AI Does Not Set Prices at McDonald's" — to dispute the claims.

"AI does not set the price of a Big Mac or any other menu item," the company wrote. "It does not change prices. And it does not determine what an individual customer pays. McDonald's does not use dynamic pricing. McDonald's provides franchisees with tools, resources, research and recommendations to help them make informed decisions. Franchisees independently set menu prices at their restaurants."

The tool, the company continued, focuses on restaurant level market dynamics that change by geographic location and follows standard business practices, such as considering local costs, competition, customer demand and economic conditions.

While the tool does offer pricing recommendations, franchisees ultimately decide what's the best value for their customers.

"A recommendation is exactly that: a recommendation, not a mandate," the company wrote. "Franchisees are not required to accept a pricing recommendation."

articles.title: Nvidia-Backed IPO’s Cratering Demand Sends Warning on AI Funding
articles.summary: The sudden plunge in demand for an Nvidia-backed data center company’s initial public offering is revealing fresh cracks in the AI funding boom.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The sudden plunge in demand for an Nvidia-backed data center company's initial public offering is revealing fresh cracks in the AI funding boom.

The planned $5.5 billion listing by Australia's Firmus Grid Ltd. has become shrouded in uncertainty after the deal failed to attract adequate support for the A$11 marketed share price, according to people familiar with the matter.

Some investors turned cautious just days after the company said it received indications of interest well above the offer size, putting it on track for a $30 billion valuation, the people said. While Firmus closed order books on Thursday, it has so far given no clear indication of the price or the deal structure, an unusual communication gap that's fueling speculation the price may be cut or the IPO scrapped altogether.

The deal underscores growing concern over how much capital AI infrastructure companies are demanding from public markets at a time when borrowing costs are rising. Much of Firmus' valuation is based on the company successfully building a pipeline of data centers across Asia serving customers such as Meta Platforms Inc. and OpenAI. Currently it operates two data centers. The IPO proceeds were needed to help fund construction of the broader network.

"Investors still believe in AI," said Maxence Visseau, Dubai-based chief investment officer at Arkevium Capital, a multi-strategy investment firm. "What they won't do is pay any price for companies that spend huge amounts on data centers, depend on a few big customers, and promise profits years from now."

Listen and follow The Bloomberg Australia Podcast on Apple, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get your podcasts.

Concerns about Firmus ranged from its lack of a proven track record to high valuations and the risk that existing shareholders could flood the market soon after listing — with about 58% of shares free to trade from day one — according to discussions with at least 10 investors and advisers. Increasing regulatory scrutiny and tighter financing conditions of data centers were also cited as a deterrent.

A representative for Firmus didn't respond to requests for comment.

UniSuper, one of Australia's biggest pension funds, was among institutional investors not taking part in the IPO.
